title: Laboratory simulation of uranium metal corrosion in different soil moisture regimes
author: Zhang, Larson, et al.

steps.title: Condition soil moisture
steps.instruction: Condition the soil at ambient temperature and humidity to the desired initial moisture content.

steps.title: Grind soil to size
steps.instruction: Grind the soil so that it passes through a 2 mm screen.

steps.title: Weigh soil and beaker
steps.instruction: Weigh the dry soil (record as W1), place it in a plastic beaker (record beaker weight as W2) that has 0.5 mm holes in the bottom.

steps.title: Capillary wetting experiment
steps.instruction: Place the beaker in a petri dish of water maintained at a depth greater than 2 cm to allow capillary water transport.

steps.title: Drain to thin water film
steps.instruction: Allow the soil to drain until the surface exhibits a thin water film, indicating capillary flow.

steps.title: Calculate saturation moisture capacity
steps.instruction: Weigh the beaker with wetted soil (record as W3) and calculate saturation moisture capacity (SMC) using SMC = (W3 − W1 − W2) / W1 × 100 %.

steps.title: Prepare glass bottles
steps.instruction: Prepare three clean wide‑mouth glass bottles and weigh each empty bottle.

steps.title: Pack soil to target bulk density
steps.instruction: Place soil in each bottle and apply force until the compactness reaches 95 % of the theoretical maximum.

steps.title: Record soil mass in bottles
steps.instruction: Weigh each bottle with soil and calculate the mass of soil contained in each bottle.

steps.title: Adjust moisture to target levels
steps.instruction: Based on the calculated soil mass, add water to achieve (a) saturation, (b) field‑capacity moisture (≈ 60 % of saturation), or (c) air‑dry (or other desired) moisture content.

steps.title: Characterize fresh uranium coupons
steps.instruction: Use X‑ray powder diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), Fourier‑transform infrared spectroscopy (FT‑IR) and Raman spectroscopy to characterize the uranium metal samples before exposure.

steps.title: Record initial uranium mass
steps.instruction: Weigh each uranium metal coupon and record its initial mass.

steps.title: Assemble corrosion device
steps.instruction: Place each uranium metal coupon into a prepared bottle and cover it with the desired thickness of overlying soil as shown in Fig. 1 (structure diagram of the corrosion device).

steps.title: Retrieve and analyze at scheduled times
steps.instruction: At each predetermined time point, remove the uranium coupon, brush off attached soil, perform XRD, SEM, FT‑IR, Raman (and any other analytical techniques) on the metal surface, and record the coupon mass.

steps.title: Repeat sampling intervals
steps.instruction: Repeat steps 13 and 14 for all required time intervals.

steps.title: Collect surrounding soil layers
steps.instruction: Dissect each system and collect soil samples from horizontal zones 0–1 cm and 2–3 cm away from the uranium coupon.

steps.title: Analyze soil and coupon
steps.instruction: Analyze the collected soil and the removed coupon using X‑ray fluorescence (XRF), XRD and any other appropriate methods.

steps.title: Perform selective sequential dissolution
steps.instruction: Apply the SSD protocol to each soil sample to determine the seven operationally defined uranium fractions; this provides uranium fractionation data for transport interpretation.

steps.title: Calculate corrosion rate
steps.instruction: Compute the corrosion rate from the measured mass loss, assuming a constant coupon surface area.

steps.title: Digest soil for total uranium (ICP‑MS)
steps.instruction: For each soil sample, weigh 21.0 g into a 50 mL digestion vessel (prepare in duplicate), add 325 mL of 4 M HNO₃, heat the mixture in a water bath at 80 °C for 16 h, filter the digest through a 0.45 µm filter, dilute the filtrate to fall within the linear range of the ICP‑MS calibration, and measure uranium concentration by ICP‑MS.

description: Production of depleted uranium (DU) metal is a means of reducing the uranium hexafluorophosphate waste produced during the process uranium enrichment. This metal has unique properties as a result of the high density and reactivity of metallic uranium. More than 17 countries are thought to have used these munitions as part of their military weapons systems [1]. In addition to military use, DU metal is used in a variety of civilian products. It is used as ballast in ships and airplanes. Boat keels, flywheels, gyroscopes and helicopter rotors are manufactured using depleted uranium. DU metal is and effective shielding material and is used as radiation shielding in radioactive material transport containers [2,3]. Kinetic energy penetrator weapons have been used in Iraq, Bosnia, Herzegovina, Kosovo/Serbia [4,5] and at military test sites in the U.S., France, Britain, Russia and Australia. When deposited in soil, the oxidation process of DU to uranium dioxide (UO2) proceeds during the weathering of metal over time. The corrosion progresses produces oxidized uranium species with lower density than the metallic DU the ratio of the molecular volume of the oxide to the molecular volume of metal, the Pilling-Bedworth [6] ratio is greater than 2 for this metal/oxide pair. Because the molecular volume of the oxide is significantly higher than the metal the oxide chips off of the metal surface exposing the underlying metal to the oxidative environment. This non-protective oxide formation continues over time. In some cases, 100 % of the metallic uranium present in soil is converted to the uranium oxide. The less oxidized U (IV) is short lived and further oxidized to U (VI) mineral. Metaschoepite (UO3·nH2O) is a primary product of DU corrosion [7,8].
